problem: The reasoning 'both are straight lines, so both are linear elements' is loose. A constant characteristic v = V or i = I is a straight line but not a proportional (through-origin) relation, and the phrase 'superposition works with them' sits next to sources in general, before dependent sources are introduced, so a student may conclude that a dependent source can be switched off in superposition — which the chapter itself later forbids.
fix: Say: 'On a v–i plot an ideal voltage source is the vertical line v = V and an ideal current source is the horizontal line i = I. Circuit theory treats an ideal independent source as a linear element, which is why the response of a linear circuit is proportional to each source value and superposition applies to independent sources. A dependent source is never switched off; only its controlling quantity is set to zero.'

problem: Only the series form of a practical source is given. The parallel form (ideal current source in parallel with R_p, terminal current I_t = I − V_t/R_p) is missing, yet it is exactly what source transformation in Chapter 1.5 needs.
fix: Add: 'A practical current source is an ideal current source in parallel with an internal resistance R_p; it supplies I − V_t/R_p to the load, so its current falls as the terminal voltage rises. A practical voltage source is the same element seen from the other side.'

problem: 'It has two output terminals like any source, plus a controlling pair' suggests a four-terminal device. The standard diamond symbol is a two-terminal element; the controlling voltage v_x or current i_x belongs to some other branch of the circuit and is only labelled next to the diamond.
fix: 'It is a two-terminal element like any source. Its value is not a number you choose: it is written in terms of a voltage v_x or a current i_x that exists in another branch, and that variable is labelled beside the diamond.'

problem: 'These four elements are the only way to write a transistor or an op-amp as a circuit element' overstates it. Small-signal models use dependent sources together with resistors and capacitors, and large-signal or behavioural models use other constructions.
fix: 'Together with resistors, capacitors and inductors, these four elements are enough to model a transistor or an op-amp, so they reappear in every amplifier problem.'

problem: 'Mixing r and g gives an answer off by a factor of ohms squared' is not meaningful. r (Ω, V/A) and g (S, A/V) are reciprocal units, so a slip gives an answer with wrong units, not one wrong by a fixed factor of ohms squared.
fix: 'Unit slips in the gain: g is in siemens (A/V), r is in ohms (V/A); they are reciprocals, r = 1/g, while μ and β are dimensionless. Carry the unit through the arithmetic: r i_x must come out in volts and g v_x in amperes, so a swapped r and g shows up as a wrong unit, not a wrong number.'
